## Objectives {.unnumbered}

This lab accompanies the Week 4 notes, [*Data Wrangling I - Loading, Cleaning and Tidying*](https://soton-fds.github.io/week04.html).

- Load delimited data files into `R` using `readr`, and check that the data has loaded correctly.
- Use `dplyr` to filter, select, mutate, arrange, group and summarise data.
- Recognise whether a dataset is tidy, and use `tidyr` to tidy it by pivoting and separating columns.
- Chain operations together into readable pipelines using `|>`.

### Task 1: Loading Data

- [x] The directory `data/part1/` contains three data files. Load them into `R` using `tidyverse`. (Hint: the three files are not all formatted in the same way.)
- [x] By default, each `read_*` function prints a message describing the columns it has read. Make sure these messages are hidden.
- [x] For each of the files, display the first few rows of the file.

::: {.solution}
```{r}
#| message: FALSE
library(tidyverse)
data1 <- read_csv("data/part1/data1.csv")
data2 <- read_delim("data/part1/data2.txt", delim = "\t")
data3 <- read_delim("data/part1/data3", delim=";")

head(data1)
head(data2)
head(data3)
```

:::

### Task 1b: Checking Loaded Data

Getting data to load without an error is only the first step: `R` will happily load data in a way that is *wrong*.
You should always check that what you have loaded makes sense.
In this task we will look more closely at the three files from Task 1.

The file `data3` contains information about books in a bookshop.

- [x] Look at the type of each column. Is the `ISBN` column stored sensibly? (Hint: an ISBN is an identifier; would it make sense to add two ISBNs together? What would happen to an ISBN that starts with a `0`?)
- [x] Reload the file so that `ISBN` is stored as text. (Hint: look up the `col_types` argument of `read_delim`, and the `cols` and `col_character` functions.)
- [x] `readr` also has a function called `read_csv2`, which reads files that use `;` as a delimiter. Try loading `data3` with `read_csv2` instead. Compare the `PriceUSD` and `AvgRating` columns to the raw file. What has gone wrong?

::: {.solution}
```{r}
data3
```
ISBN is a double, which is a number so it can be added together however as it should be an identifier it should be loaded as text. If it starts with a zero the number stored will not be the correct ISBN.
```{r}
data3 <- read_delim("data/part1/data3", delim=";", col_types =(cols(ISBN = col_character())))
data3
```
It is working now! I learnt `col_select()` makes the table reduce to just the column I selected. Now we break the data again:
```{r}
#| message: FALSE
data3AU <-read_csv2("data/part1/data3", col_types =(cols(ISBN = col_character())) )
data3AU
```

Oh no it has loaded the prices and the average rating as ignoring the decimal point.
:::

The file `data1.csv` contains student scores from two tests, with their average.

- [x] How are missing scores recorded in the raw file, and what do they become when loaded into `R`? What else in the file was loaded as missing?
- [x] Compute the mean of `score1`. Why do you get `NA`, and how can you fix this? (Hint: look at how `na.rm` was used in the notes.)
- [ ] Look at the row for Henry Zhao. Are his scores really `0`? What happens to the mean of `score1` and of `average` if he is excluded?

::: {.solution}
Lets see what's wrong with data1
```{r}
data1
```
Missing values are loaded into `R` as `NA`.The other thing that is missing is a message about Ivy Chen.

Let's have a go at computing the mean:
```{r}
mean(data1$score1)
```
Would you look at that it comes out as `NA` as it said it would! Now lets fix:
```{r}
mean(data1$score1, na.rm=TRUE)
```
It works now!!!!

Henry Zhao was absent so his scores should not count in the calculating of the mean values for score one. How do we exclude??
```{r}
mean(data1$score1[data1$name != "Henry Zhao"], na.rm= TRUE)
```
This has dramatically increased the class average.

:::

The file `data2.txt` contains readings from air quality monitoring stations.

- [x] Create a `tibble` containing only `station_id` and the particulate matter readings (the columns measured in µg/m³). Use a tidyselect helper rather than typing out the column names.

::: {.solution}
First see what data we are looking at for the column names and types
```{r}
data2
```

```{r}
data2 |> select(station_id, ends_with("m3"))
```

:::

- [x] How many readings are there in the file, and from how many different neighbourhoods? (Hint: look at the "Other Summarise Functions" tip in the notes.)

::: {.solution}
I did this already in the assessment. Starting to see that completing the lab before the assessment might be a good idea. 

```{r}
data2 |> summarise(n_readings = n(), n_neighbourhoods = n_distinct(neighborhood))
```
:::

- [x] Which readings have a `status` other than `OK`? What do you notice about their pollution readings and `sensor_uptime_pct`?
- [ ] Compute the mean `pm2_5_ug_m3` over all readings, and over only the readings with status `OK`. Which would you report, and why?

::: {.solution}
First box we do first: status other than okay with columns for pollution readings and `sensor_uptime_pct`.

```{r}
data2 |> filter( status != "OK") |> select(status,sensor_uptime_pct,  ends_with("m3"))
```
I notice that one of them is an error so there are no values for pollution and the `sensor_uptime_pct` is only 60 which could be why is error. I don't know why the other ones are weird.

Now for computing the mean accross all:
```{r}
data2 |> summarise(mean_pollution = mean(pm2_5_ug_m3, na.rm = TRUE))
```
Now for just those who's status is OK:
```{r}
data2 |> filter(status != "OK") |> summarise(mean_pollution = mean(pm2_5_ug_m3, na.rm = TRUE))
```
The mean has gone up. 
:::

### Task 2: `dplyr`

The `diamonds` dataset is included as a part of `ggplot2`.
If you have loaded `tidyverse` it should be already in your environment.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
diamonds
```

It contains information about `r nrow(diamonds)` diamonds.
Each row is a diamond, and each column contains information about that diamond such as:

- `price`: The price of the diamond in US dollars.
- `carat`: The weight of the diamond (1 carat = 0.2g).
- `cut`: Quality of the cut.
- `color`: The color of the diamond.
- `clarity`: A measure of how clear the diamond is.
- `depth`: Total depth percentage; $= \frac{z}{\frac{1}{2}(x + y)} \times 100$.
- `table`: Width of the top of the diamond relative to the widest point.
- `x`: Length of the diamond in mm.
- `y`: Width of the diamond in mm.
- `z`: Depth of the diamond in mm.

For the next few tasks you should use `dplyr` functions, using pipe syntax.
Try to format your code nicely so it is readable.


- [x] Add a new column to the `tibble` called `volume` that contains the volume of the diamond ($x \times y \times z$).

::: {.solution}
```{r}
diamonds <- diamonds |> mutate(volume = x*y*z)
diamonds
```

:::

- [x] Create a `tibble` containing only the numeric columns of `diamonds`. (Hint: look at the tidyselect callout in the notes.)

::: {.solution}
```{r}
diamonds2 <- diamonds |> select(where(is.numeric))
diamonds2
```
:::

Now answer the following research questions.

- [x] What is the average price of all the diamonds in the dataset?
- [x] What is the volume of the 5 highest priced diamonds?
- [x] What is the average, minimum and maximum price of diamonds for each cut?
- [x] Ideal is the best cut, yet it has the lowest average price. Can you explain why? (Hint: compare the average `carat` of each cut.)
- [x] For each cut, what is the average price-per-carat for diamonds with that cut?
- [x] What are the most common combinations of cut and colour? (Hint: look up the `count` function)
- [x] Create a `tibble` containing diamonds that are "unusually" large (having volume more than three standard deviations from the mean volume)?

::: {.solution}
Here are my answers to the above research questions:

Average price:
```{r}
diamonds|> summarise(price_mean=mean(price) )
```

Volume of highest priced:
```{r}
diamonds |> select(volume, price) |> arrange(desc(price))
```
The volume of the 5 highest priced diamonds are: 371.4942, 317.3335, 249.0294,	340.6633, 318.6360.

The average, minimum and maximum price of diamonds for each cut:
```{r}
diamonds |> group_by(cut) |> summarise ( mean = mean(price), maximum = max(price), minimum = min(price)) |> arrange(desc(mean))
```

Why is Ideal the averagely lowest price?
```{r}
diamonds |> group_by(cut) |> summarise ( mean_price = mean(price), mean_carat = mean(carat))|> arrange(desc(mean_price))
```

Average price per carat:
```{r}
diamonds |> group_by(cut) |> summarise ( mean_price = mean(price), mean_carat = mean(carat))|> mutate( average_price_per_carat = mean_price/mean_carat) |> arrange(desc(average_price_per_carat))
```

Most common combinations of cut and colour:
```{r}
diamonds |> group_by(cut) |> count(color) |> arrange(desc(n))
```
The most common combinations of cut and colour are Ideal with G then E then F then H. 

Table with unusually large diamonds:
```{r}
diamonds |> filter (volume > (3*sd(volume) + mean(volume)))
```

:::

Before trusting these results, it is worth checking whether they make sense. Since all diamonds have the same density, heavier diamonds are larger, so `carat` and `volume` should be closely related.

- [x] Look at the largest few diamonds in your answer. Given their `carat`, are their volumes plausible?
- [x] Add a new column called `volume_per_carat` containing the ratio of `volume` to `carat`. Look at the diamonds with the smallest and largest values of this ratio. Does this suggest there any errors in the dataset?
- [x] Create a new `tibble` called `diamonds_clean` that keeps only diamonds with `volume_per_carat` between 100 and 250. How many diamonds did you remove?
- [x] Repeat the "unusually large" question using `diamonds_clean`. How many diamonds do you find now, and why has the number changed?

::: {.solution}
Given the carat is tiny with the last volumes of diamonds the volumes given are definitely not plausible. 
checking volume per carat:
```{r}
diamonds3 <- diamonds |> mutate(volume_per_carat = volume/carat) |> arrange(volume_per_carat)

diamonds |> mutate(volume_per_carat = volume/carat) |> arrange(desc(volume_per_carat))
```
This definitely suggests there are mistakes in the data set. 

New tibble with clean data:
```{r}
diamonds_clean = diamonds3 |> filter (volume_per_carat <= 250 & volume_per_carat >= 100)
diamonds_clean
```
I removed 39 rows.

Trying the unusually large diamonds thing now:
```{r}
diamonds_clean |> filter (volume > (3*sd(volume) + mean(volume)))
```

I have more diamonds in this data set because the mean has reduced in size by a lot and so has the standard deviation so more diamonds sit outside of it. 
:::

- [x] **Extension:** Find the most expensive diamond of each cut.

::: {.solution}
```{r}
 diamonds_clean |> group_by(cut) |> summarise(maximum_price = max(price))
```
most expensive diamond for each cut:
```{r}
diamonds_clean |> filter( price == 18574	| price == 18707	| price == 18818	| price == 18823 | price == 18806	)
```
:::


### Task 3: `tidyr`

The file `data/part3/assessment.csv` contains a messy student scores table.
It records the student's scores out of 100 across 8 possible assessments.
However, not all students take all assessments, and assessments the student has not taken are recorded as `NA`.

- [ ] Load the file and look at it. Recall the three rules of tidy data from the notes. Is this table tidy? If not, which rule(s) does it break?

::: {.solution}

:::

- [ ] Tidy the table: pivot into long format with one row per student and assessment, and drop missing scores.
- [ ] Compute each student's overall average, and the number of assessments they took. (Hint: look at the "Other Summarise Functions" tip in the notes.)

::: {.solution}

:::

- [ ] Redo the pivot, this time using `starts_with` to choose the columns to pivot. Check you get the same result. Suppose a new column `student_name` were added to the file: which of the two approaches would still work, and why?

::: {.solution}

:::

One of the key principles of tidy data is that each cell should contain only one value.
Notice that in the new dataset, the column `assessment` contains *two* values: the Semester and the Assessment ID,
separated by an `_`.

- [ ] Use `separate_wider_delim` to split `assessment` into two columns, one with the assessment ID and one with the Semester.
- [ ] Create a wide table with one row per student, and two new columns containing the average score in Semester 1 and Semester 2.

::: {.solution}

:::

- [ ] Add a column `improvement` to the wide table showing how much each student's average score changed from Semester 1 to Semester 2. Which students improved the most, and which declined the most?

::: {.solution}

:::

- [ ] **Extension:** We tidied this dataset in two steps: `pivot_longer` followed by `separate_wider_delim`. Can you do both in a single call to `pivot_longer`? (Hint: look at the `names_sep` argument in `?pivot_longer`.)

::: {.solution}

:::
